title: On Display, On Fyah & Feelin’ Jovani: ‘The Real Housewives’ & Andy Cohen Take Us Inside 20 Years of Bravo-Fueled Music
summary: Housewives past & present look back on their most iconic songs to celebrate Bravo's milestone anniversary.
contentText:
Don’t be tardy for the (anniversary) party!

For the past 20 years, the Real Housewives franchise has dominated pop culture as the go-to reality TV institution for catty drama, aspirational wealth and navigating the ever-complicated social politics of female friendship.

Related

RHOSLC’s Whitney Rose Prompts Hilarious Response From Rihanna After Saying She’s Sad Because ‘We Still Haven’t Had Any New Music’

Ex-‘RHOBH’ Star Brandi Glanville Drops Her First Song, ‘Life of a Housewife’

Now, more than two decades after a little experiment called The Real Housewives of Orange County first premiered, Bravo is commemorating the landmark milestone with The Real Housewives Ultimate Girls Trip: Roaring 20th , a nine-episode anniversary series celebrating all the iconic women who’ve graced our screens from New York City and Atlanta to Beverly Hills, Miami and beyond. (New episodes premiere Sunday nights on Bravo at 9 p.m. ET/PT and start streaming the next day on Peacock.)

Many of the women who’ve redefined what it means to be a “Housewife” in front of Bravo’s cameras have also turned their exploits into a catalog of quotable, clubby musical earworms. As Porsha Williams, the Real Housewives of Atlanta mainstay representing Georgia’s peaches on the new season of RHUGT , quipped during the third episode of the anniversary special, “If a Housewife gon’ do anything, they’re gonna be confident as a singer , honey.”

But before Bravoholics were singing along to “Tardy for the Party” or “Chic C’est La Vie,” a girl from Southern California was the original Real Housewife to turn her reality TV ambitions into dreams of pop stardom.

U Can’t Control Jo

Back in 2007, Jo De La Rosa was an original cast member of The Real Housewives of Orange County . At just 26 years old, she was filming her second season of the show that would soon launch franchises across the country and start a pop culture phenomenon that would define the 21st century.

From the start, De La Rosa stood out from her fellow First Ladies of Bravo. Younger than her castmates by nearly two decades, the then-engaged daughter of musician Juan Carlos Contreras already had her sights set far beyond the cloistered gates of Coto De Caza — the exclusive gated community in sunny southern California where Bravo had inadvertently struck gold.

“I was going to L.A. a lot with my girlfriends on the weekends, meeting a lot of people, and producers happened to know that I was trying to get into the world of [music],” she tells Billboard — adding that, in actuality, her goal was not to become the next Britney Spears or Christina Aguilera, but to write for them. 

“Really, my dream in my entire 20s was to move to L.A. and get a publishing deal. I wanted to be a songwriter,” she confesses — citing Kara DioGuardi, who spent much of the 2000s penning hit after hit for the aforementioned pop princesses, as well as Kelly Clarkson, Hilary Duff, P!nk and more, as a major inspiration. “That was my dream. I wanted to get signed to a music publishing house and be background writing for really big pop artists.”

However, after a chance meeting with rapper Won-G at a Los Angeles eatery on one of those girls’ weekends, De La Rosa found herself rather unexpectedly in front of the microphone rather than in the liner notes. Over the course of RHOC ’s second season, the aspiring songwriter found herself in meetings with Grammy-winning producer Bob Cutarella and recording a demo in the famed studios of Capitol Records — all as cameras followed her every move.

“ So intimidating,” De La Rosa says of the experience with a self-conscious laugh. “I felt like such an impostor! Because it’s like, who am I , first of all? Some girl from O.C. on some show where cameras follow them around. Like, ‘How dare I step into these studios to record!’”

After just two seasons, De La Rosa left RHOC with demo in hand to pursue her music career in L.A., eventually signing a record deal and releasing her debut album, Unscripted , in 2008. (She also achieved what she calls the “biggest accomplishment” of her music career when one of her self-penned album cuts, “Rumors,” was featured in a 2008 episode of another Y2K-era reality juggernaut, MTV’s The Hills .) 

The fan-favorite Housewife continued to make cameos on the show over the next couple of seasons — including filming the music video for her single “U Can’t Control Me” in Season 4’s history-making “Bass Lake” episode — but she admits in hindsight that her attempt at a music career was more happenstance than planned out step by strategic step.

“We didn’t really have an example of what ‘reality’ was [at the time],” she says. “I know times have changed, but there was no forethought, there was no planning, there was no thinking ahead in terms of, like, chatter at the network. I was so naive, because it was so early on. I was kind of just showing up and shooting, and whatever producers caught, they caught.”

Making a Kandi Koated Classic

For his part, Bravo’s Andy Cohen also views De La Rosa’s foray making music as more of a precursor to the trend on Housewives rather than its official start. 

“It seemed at the time like she was doing it for fun,” the longtime executive producer, perennial reunion host and face of the network tells Billboard from his office at Bravo’s headquarters in Midtown Manhattan. “I forgot that Jo was actually our first ‘recording artist!’”

While the RHOC OG was certainly a Housewives trailblazer, it’s safe to say Bravo went multi-platinum when Kandi Burruss, a member of the ‘90s girl group Xscape, joined The Real Housewives of Atlanta in 2009. 

In her first season as a Housewife, the R&B powerhouse — who also later became the the Grammy-winning songwriter behind turn-of-the-millennium hits like TLC’s “No Scrubs” and Destiny’s Child’s “Bills, Bills, Bills” — brought a serious dose of industry credibility (and a world of new musical possibilities) to RHOA ’s juiciest peaches.

Recruited by cast mate Kim Zolciak, Burruss helped write and produce her new pal’s debut single, “Tardy for the Party,” and the dance-pop bop quickly became the first truly inescapable novelty hit within the Bravoverse. With its sing-song hook, club-ready production and heavy use of AutoTune to make up for the wig-loving Zolciak’s lack of formal training, the catchy track was never likely to dominate top 40 radio, but it created a template that many a Housewife would follow in the future.

“I think after Kim recorded ‘Tardy for the Party,’ it opened the floodgates,” Cohen says, readily citing the song as his pick for the most iconic musical moment in Housewives history. “It started everything, and it was the beginning of seeing a Housewife who wasn’t an actual singer try to do it.” 

“Tardy” also provided seasons’ worth of fodder for The Real Housewives of Atlanta ’s central storyline. At the Season 2 reunion, Zolciak and Burruss debuted the song live for the first time as their fellow ‘Wives looked on; the following season, they jetted off to the West Coast to perform at the Palm Springs White Party in front of a crowd of 10,000 gay fans. 

Soon enough, though, drama surrounding the song took a turn for the worse, with the pair falling out over financial compensation and royalties from the song — a central conflict that extended across multiple seasons, before Zolciak abruptly quit the series just a few weeks into filming Season 5 in 2012. (Burruss, meanwhile, would remain a staple on the show for nearly 15 years, becoming the longest-running Atlanta Housewife, before exiting in 2023.)
